column3: The word for "I" and "me": Chinese does not change the pronoun between subject and object, so 我 is the same in 我看他 and 他看我. 我 began as a picture of a trident-like weapon (perhaps a three-bladed polearm, two scholars suggest) and was borrowed for its sound to write "I" as early as the oracle bones.
column9: The word for "I" and "me": Chinese does not change the pronoun between subject and object, so 我 is the same in 我看他 and 他看我. 我 began as a picture of a trident-like weapon (perhaps a three-bladed polearm, two scholars suggest) and was borrowed for its sound to write "I" as early as the oracle bones.

column3: You. The 亻 (person) gives the meaning and 尔 probably gives the sound; the same 亻 starts 他, 们 and 住. For more than one person add 们: 你们. For someone you want to treat with respect there is 您.
column9: You. The 亻 (person) gives the meaning and 尔 probably gives the sound; the same 亻 starts 他, 們 and 住. For more than one person add 們: 你們. For someone you want to treat with respect there is 您.

column3: Said tā like 她 and 它, so only context tells them apart in speech. In 他人 and 他乡 it is a bound form meaning “other”. The “he, she, it” sense came after the Han period and replaced classical 其 and 之.
column9: Said tā like 她 and 它, so only context tells them apart in speech. In 他人 and 他鄉 it is a bound form meaning “other”. The “he, she, it” sense came after the Han period and replaced classical 其 and 之.

column3: Said tā exactly like 他 and 它, so only the writing tells a woman from a man. It can also be used for something beloved, such as a country, in speeches and poems.
column9: Said tā exactly like 他 and 它, so only the writing tells a woman from a man. It can also be used for something beloved, such as a country, in speeches and poems.

column3: Polite “you” for one person, to elders, customers, strangers. For a group say 您几位 or 您二位, not 您们. When 您 first appeared in the Jin and Yuan eras, it served as singular and plural.
column9: Polite “you” for one person, to elders, customers, strangers. For a group say 您幾位 or 您二位, not 您們. When 您 first appeared in the Jin and Yuan eras, it served as singular and plural.

column3: The plural of people words: 我们, 同学们, 孩子们, 先生们. It does not go with a number (三个孩子) and never with things, so not 书们. As a plural marker 们 is a late arrival, first attested in the Song dynasty.
column9: The plural of people words: 我們, 同學們, 孩子們, 先生們. It does not go with a number (三個孩子) and never with things, so not 書們. As a plural marker 們 is a late arrival, first attested in the Song dynasty.

column3: It can leave the listener out, while 咱们 always includes them: a seller saying 我们 means the shop, not you. Add 的 for “our”: 我们的老师. 我 began as a trident-like weapon, borrowed for the sound of “I”; the hand holding a weapon is a folk etymology.
column9: It can leave the listener out, while 咱們 always includes them: a seller saying 我們 means the shop, not you. Add 的 for “our”: 我們的老師. 我 began as a trident-like weapon, borrowed for the sound of “I”; the hand holding a weapon is a folk etymology.

column3: Plural “you”, for two or more people: 你们好 greets a group. Add 的 for “your”: 你们的老师. There is no polite plural 您们; say 您几位. 你 is a colloquial word attested since the Tang dynasty.
column9: Plural “you”, for two or more people: 你們好 greets a group. Add 的 for “your”: 你們的老師. There is no polite plural 您們; say 您幾位. 你 is a colloquial word attested since the Tang dynasty.

column3: Used for a mixed group or men alone, even when only one man is among women. All women is 她们, things are 它们; all are said tāmen. 他 is sometimes read tuō in literary contexts, for its classical “other” sense.
column9: Used for a mixed group or men alone, even when only one man is among women. All women is 她們, things are 它們; all are said tāmen. 他 is sometimes read tuō in literary contexts, for its classical “other” sense.

column3: Only for a group of women or girls; one man in the group makes it 他们. All the forms are said tāmen, so the difference is only in writing.
column9: Only for a group of women or girls; one man in the group makes it 他們. All the forms are said tāmen, so the difference is only in writing.

column3: Good or "well", and on its own the answer "OK, fine". It is 女 (woman) and 子 (child); the usual explanation is that a woman with a child was seen as good. Read hǎo here; as "to like" it is read hào, as in 爱好.
column7: The weather is very nice today.
column9: Good or "well", and on its own the answer "OK, fine". It is 女 (woman) and 子 (child); the usual explanation is that a woman with a child was seen as good. Read hǎo here; as "to like" it is read hào, as in 愛好.

column3: The light, everyday thanks; the second 谢 is neutral. Add the person or thing: 谢谢你, 谢谢大家. The usual answer is 不客气. 谢 also means to refuse and, of flowers, to wither.
column9: The light, everyday thanks; the second 謝 is neutral. Add the person or thing: 謝謝你, 謝謝大家. The usual answer is 不客氣. 謝 also means to refuse and, of flowers, to wither.

column3: The usual answer to thanks. Said earlier as 请不要客气 it means “make yourself at home”; and 对他不客气 is to treat someone bluntly. 不 began as a picture of a flower’s calyx, and took on “no” later.
column9: The usual answer to thanks. Said earlier as 請不要客氣 it means “make yourself at home”; and 對他不客氣 is to treat someone bluntly. 不 began as a picture of a flower’s calyx, and took on “no” later.

column3: Sorry, for a mistake or for bumping into someone: it says you have let the other person down, the opposite of 对得起. The usual answer is 没关系; 不好意思 is a lighter "sorry". It is not used for sympathy, as in "I'm sorry to hear that".
column9: Sorry, for a mistake or for bumping into someone: it says you have let the other person down, the opposite of 對得起. The usual answer is 沒關係; 不好意思 is a lighter "sorry". It is not used for sympathy, as in "I'm sorry to hear that".

column3: The usual answer to 对不起; 没事 and 不要紧 say the same. It also means “makes no difference”: 去不去没关系. 跟…没关系 means nothing to do with. As mò, 没 means “drowned/to end/to die/to inundate”.
column9: The usual answer to 對不起; 沒事 and 不要緊 say the same. It also means “makes no difference”: 去不去沒關係. 跟…沒關係 means nothing to do with. As mò, 沒 means “drowned/to end/to die/to inundate”.

column3: Waves off thanks or an apology. Before a noun or adjective it means “not much of a”: 没什么人, 没什么意思. 么 is a variant of 幺 (yāo), the spoken “one” in phone numbers.
column9: Waves off thanks or an apology. Before a noun or adjective it means “not much of a”: 沒什麼人, 沒什麼意思.

column3: The standard goodbye. A time before 见 says when: 明天见, 一会儿见, 周一见. Casually people say 拜拜. 见 is also read xiàn, “to appear”.
column9: The standard goodbye. A time before 見 says when: 明天見, 一會兒見, 週一見. Casually people say 拜拜. 見 is also read xiàn, “to appear”.

column3: Before a verb it asks politely: 请坐. It also covers inviting and hiring: 请客 is to treat guests, 请假 to ask for leave, 请老师 to hire a teacher.
column9: Before a verb it asks politely: 請坐. It also covers inviting and hiring: 請客 is to treat guests, 請假 to ask for leave, 請老師 to hire a teacher.

column3: Said before the question, to a stranger or someone you respect. Among friends a plain question will do; in an argument 请问 sounds sharp, as in “and just how…?”. 问 is related to the word for “to hear”, literally “let (me) hear”.
column7: Excuse me, where is the restroom?
column9: Said before the question, to a stranger or someone you respect. Among friends a plain question will do; in an argument 請問 sounds sharp, as in “and just how…?”. 問 is related to the word for “to hear”, literally “let (me) hear”.

column3: A host’s words to someone at the door; 请进来 is as common. 进来 is coming in toward the speaker, 进去 going in away from them. 进 pictures a bird that can only walk forward, never backward.
column7: Please come in and sit down.
column9: A host’s words to someone at the door; 請進來 is as common. 進來 is coming in toward the speaker, 進去 going in away from them. 進 pictures a bird that can only walk forward, never backward.

column3: A host or teacher offering a seat, with the place after it: 请坐这里. 坐 also means to travel on: 坐车, 坐飞机.
column9: A host or teacher offering a seat, with the place after it: 請坐這裡. 坐 also means to travel on: 坐車, 坐飛機.

column3: It is said yí before a fourth tone (一个) and yì before the others (一天), but keeps yī in counting and dates. Phone numbers often say yāo to avoid a mix-up with qī.
column9: It is said yí before a fourth tone (一個) and yì before the others (一天), but keeps yī in counting and dates. Phone numbers often say yāo to avoid a mix-up with qī.

column3: Use 二 for counting, numbers, dates and ordinals (二十, 第二, 二月), but 两 before a measure word: 两个人. In some Mandarin dialects 二 also means silly.
column6: Jīntiān shì èr yuè èr hào.
column9: Use 二 for counting, numbers, dates and ordinals (二十, 第二, 二月), but 兩 before a measure word: 兩個人. In some Mandarin dialects 二 also means silly.

column3: Often “a few”: 三五个 is three or five, 再三 again and again, 三思而行 think twice. A number goes before a measure word: 三本书.
column9: Often “a few”: 三五個 is three or five, 再三 again and again, 三思而行 think twice. A number goes before a measure word: 三本書.

column3: Unlucky, since it sounds like 死: many buildings skip a fourth floor. 四 began as a picture of a nose exhaling, later borrowed for “four” by sound; the older four-stroke form 亖 was easy to mix up with 二 and 三 in vertical writing.
column9: Unlucky, since it sounds like 死: many buildings skip a fourth floor. 四 began as a picture of a nose exhaling, later borrowed for “four” by sound; the older four-stroke form 亖 was easy to mix up with 二 and 三 in vertical writing.

column3: Days count up from 星期一, so 星期五 is Friday. It also grades quality: 五星级 is a five-star hotel. Its origin is unclear; one scholar suggests a tally mark, another the palm lines of a hand.
column6: Wǒ jiā yǒu wǔ kǒu rén.
column7: There are five people in my family.
column9: Days count up from 星期一, so 星期五 is Friday. It also grades quality: 五星級 is a five-star hotel. Its origin is unclear; one scholar suggests a tally mark, another the palm lines of a hand.

column3: A lucky number: 六六大顺 wishes that all goes smoothly, and 66 or 666 is a favored amount in gifts. Saturday is 星期六. 六 was perhaps a picture of a shed.
column9: A lucky number: 六六大順 wishes that all goes smoothly, and 66 or 666 is a favored amount in gifts. Saturday is 星期六. 六 was perhaps a picture of a shed.

column3: It sits in 七夕, the seventh day of the seventh month, a Chinese Valentine’s Day, and in 七上八下, a nervous flutter. 七 is a vertical and a horizontal stroke crossing, the original character of 切, “to cut”.
column9: It sits in 七夕, the seventh day of the seventh month, a Chinese Valentine’s Day, and in 七上八下, a nervous flutter. 七 is a vertical and a horizontal stroke crossing, the original character of 切, “to cut”.

column3: Eight. It is two bent lines meaning "to divide", later borrowed for the number because of the sound. The idea of dividing is still visible in 半 and 分, which both contain 八.
column9: Eight. It is two bent lines meaning "to divide", later borrowed for the number because of the sound. The idea of dividing is still visible in 半 and 分, which both contain 八.

column3: It sounds like 久 “long-lasting”, so it is lucky, and as the largest single digit it can mean “most”: 十有八九 is most likely. 九 began as an elbow, a word now written 肘.
column9: It sounds like 久 “long-lasting”, so it is lucky, and as the largest single digit it can mean “most”: 十有八九 is most likely. 九 began as an elbow, a word now written 肘.

column3: Ten: a crossing of a horizontal and a vertical stroke; early forms were a single vertical stroke and the origin is debated. 11-19 are 十 plus a digit (十一), 20-90 a digit plus 十 (二十).
column9: Ten: a crossing of a horizontal and a vertical stroke; early forms were a single vertical stroke and the origin is debated. 11-19 are 十 plus a digit (十一), 20-90 a digit plus 十 (二十).

column3: In a number one 零 fills any gap: 105 is 一百零五, and 1005 is 一千零五. It also means small bits: 零钱 small change, 零食 snacks. 零 first meant a little bit of rain; in 1248 Li Ye used it as a placeholder.
column6: Zhè běn shū yībǎi líng wǔ kuài.
column9: In a number one 零 fills any gap: 105 is 一百零五, and 1005 is 一千零五. It also means small bits: 零錢 small change, 零食 snacks. 零 first meant a little bit of rain; in 1248 Li Ye used it as a placeholder.

column3: It is written for the digits of a year or a phone number, read one by one: 二〇二五年 is èr líng èr wǔ nián. In a quantity with a gap, 零 is the form: 一百零五. It is a plain circle, used for a zero digit in numbers since at least the 12th century.
column6: Wǒ èr líng líng líng nián chūshēng.
column9: It is written for the digits of a year or a phone number, read one by one: 二〇二五年 is èr líng èr wǔ nián. In a quantity with a gap, 零 is the form: 一百零五. It is a plain circle, used for a zero digit in numbers since at least the 12th century.

column3: Before a measure word 两 is the form, not 二: 两个人, 两本书. 二 stays for counting, numbers and ordinals (二十, 第二). 两 also means a couple: 过两天, 两三个.
column9: Before a measure word 兩 is the form, not 二: 兩個人, 兩本書. 二 stays for counting, numbers and ordinals (二十, 第二). 兩 also means a couple: 過兩天, 兩三個.

column3: At the start of a number it needs 一: say 一百, not just 百. A skipped place inside a number takes 零: 一百零五. In speech 一百二 is shorthand for 120.
column6: Zhè ge bēizi yī bǎi kuài.
column7: This cup is a hundred yuan.
column9: At the start of a number it needs 一: say 一百, not just 百. A skipped place inside a number takes 零: 一百零五. In speech 一百二 is shorthand for 120.

column3: It guesses a small number, ten or fewer, and takes a measure word: 几个人, 几本书. For larger or open quantities use 多少. It also asks 几点 (what time), 几月, 几岁. It began as a picture of a small stool seen from the side.
column7: How many friends do you have?
column9: It guesses a small number, ten or fewer, and takes a measure word: 幾個人, 幾本書. For larger or open quantities use 多少. It also asks 幾點 (what time), 幾月, 幾歲. It began as a picture of a small stool seen from the side.

column3: It asks any amount and needs no measure word: 多少钱, 多少人. Said duōshǎo, it means somewhat: 多少有点累. For a small number you expect, 几 is used instead. 多 was two pieces of meat, not two nights: the 肉 turned into 夕 by looking alike.
column9: It asks any amount and needs no measure word: 多少錢, 多少人. Said duōshǎo, it means somewhat: 多少有點累. For a small number you expect, 幾 is used instead. 多 was two pieces of meat, not two nights: the 肉 turned into 夕 by looking alike.

column3: It goes before a measure word: 半个小时, 半杯水. But "an hour and a half" puts it after: 一个半小时. 三点半 is half past three, 一半 is one half. It shows 八, divide, over 牛, a cow: cutting a cow in half.
column9: It goes before a measure word: 半個小時, 半杯水. But "an hour and a half" puts it after: 一個半小時. 三點半 is half past three, 一半 is one half. It shows 八, divide, over 牛, a cow: cutting a cow in half.

column3: Put before a number it makes an ordinal: 第一, 第二次, 第三名. Dates and months take the bare number instead: 三月, 三号, never 第三月.
column6: Zhè shì wǒ dì yī cì lái.
column7: This is my first time here.
column9: Put before a number it makes an ordinal: 第一, 第二次, 第三名. Dates and months take the bare number instead: 三月, 三號, never 第三月.

column3: Added to a place or kind it names the person: 中国人, 老人, 工人, 女人. 别人 means other people. The measure word is 个, or 位 for respect: 三位客人. It is a side view of a standing man, with an arm and a leg; on the left of other characters it shrinks to 亻.
column7: There are a lot of people here.
column9: Added to a place or kind it names the person: 中國人, 老人, 工人, 女人. 別人 means other people. The measure word is 個, or 位 for respect: 三位客人. It is a side view of a standing man, with an arm and a leg; on the left of other characters it shrinks to 亻.

column3: Male. 田 (field) over 力 (strength): it is read as the person who supplies the strength to work a field. It pairs with 女, and starts 男人, 男生 and 男朋友.
column9: Male. 田 (field) over 力 (strength): it is read as the person who supplies the strength to work a field. It pairs with 女, and starts 男人, 男生 and 男朋友.

column3: It marks the female counterpart in words: 女儿, 女朋友, 女人, 女老师. Typed nv on a keyboard. It is a picture of a woman with folded arms, kneeling or standing.
column6: Tā shì yī wèi nǚ yīshēng.
column9: It marks the female counterpart in words: 女兒, 女朋友, 女人, 女老師. Typed nv on a keyboard. It is a picture of a woman with folded arms, kneeling or standing.

column3: Used alone to call to her (妈，我回来了) or after 我 (我妈). 妈妈 is the fuller everyday word; 大妈 is a polite name for a woman of your parents' age. It is a colloquial form of 母, the character for mother.
column9: Used alone to call to her (媽，我回來了) or after 我 (我媽). 媽媽 is the fuller everyday word; 大媽 is a polite name for a woman of your parents' age. It is a colloquial form of 母, the character for mother.

column3: Family terms are often doubled (爸爸, 哥哥, 姐姐), with a light second syllable. Chinese says 爸爸妈妈, father first, where English says "mom and dad". 妈 is a colloquial form of 母.
column9: Family terms are often doubled (爸爸, 哥哥, 姐姐), with a light second syllable. Chinese says 爸爸媽媽, father first, where English says "mom and dad". 媽 is a colloquial form of 母.

column3: Used alone to call to him (爸，你在哪儿？) or after 我 (我爸). 爸爸 is the fuller word, and 爸妈 means both parents. 老爸 is a casual "my old man". It is a colloquial form of 父, and unlike 父 it keeps the lip sound b of the old word.
column9: Used alone to call to him (爸，你在哪兒？) or after 我 (我爸). 爸爸 is the fuller word, and 爸媽 means both parents. 老爸 is a casual "my old man". It is a colloquial form of 父, and unlike 父 it keeps the lip sound b of the old word.

column3: The everyday spoken word, with a light second syllable: bàba. It is used to call to him and to speak of him; 父亲 is the written, formal word. 爸 is a colloquial form of 父.
column9: The everyday spoken word, with a light second syllable: bàba. It is used to call to him and to speak of him; 父親 is the written, formal word. 爸 is a colloquial form of 父.

column3: Older brother. It is two 可 stacked; the character first meant "to sing, song" and the sense "older brother" is a later borrowing. The "song" meaning survives in 歌, which has 哥 as its sound part.
column6: Wǒ gē bǐ wǒ dà sān suì.
column7: My older brother is three years older than me.
column9: Older brother. It is two 可 stacked; the character first meant "to sing, song" and the sense "older brother" is a later borrowing. The "song" meaning survives in 歌, which has 哥 as its sound part.

column3: Chinese always says older or younger: 哥哥 and 姐姐 are older, 弟弟 and 妹妹 younger. 哥 alone is an address after a name or for a young man you respect. 哥 is two 可 stacked, and a clipping of 阿哥, a borrowing from Xianbei.
column7: My older brother works in Beijing.
column9: Chinese always says older or younger: 哥哥 and 姐姐 are older, 弟弟 and 妹妹 younger. 哥 alone is an address after a name or for a young man you respect. 哥 is two 可 stacked, and a clipping of 阿哥, a borrowing from Xianbei.

column3: Alone it is mostly an address after a name (小红姐) or part of a word: 小姐, 空姐, 姐妹. For your own sister, 姐姐 is the everyday word, though 我姐 is fine.
column7: My older sister is a teacher.
column9: Alone it is mostly an address after a name (小紅姐) or part of a word: 小姐, 空姐, 姐妹. For your own sister, 姐姐 is the everyday word, though 我姐 is fine.

column3: With a light second syllable: jiějie. It is also what you call a young woman a little older than you who is no relative. In a big family, 大姐 is the eldest sister.
column7: My older sister is taller than me.
column9: With a light second syllable: jiějie. It is also what you call a young woman a little older than you who is no relative. In a big family, 大姐 is the eldest sister.

column3: Alone it appears in 我弟, in compounds such as 兄弟 and 师弟, and as an address to a younger boy. In old letters a man modestly calls himself 弟. It began as a spear handle wrapped in a leather strap; the wrapping meant order, and that stretched to "younger brother".
column7: My younger brother is at school.
column9: Alone it appears in 我弟, in compounds such as 兄弟 and 師弟, and as an address to a younger boy. In old letters a man modestly calls himself 弟. It began as a spear handle wrapped in a leather strap; the wrapping meant order, and that stretched to "younger brother".

column3: With a light second syllable: dìdi. It is also what you call a boy a bit younger than you. In the pair 哥哥 and 弟弟 Chinese always says older or younger. 弟 began as a spear handle wrapped in a strap; the wrapping meant order.
column6: Dìdi bǐ wǒ xiǎo liǎng suì.
column7: My younger brother is two years younger than me.
column9: With a light second syllable: dìdi. It is also what you call a boy a bit younger than you. In the pair 哥哥 and 弟弟 Chinese always says older or younger. 弟 began as a spear handle wrapped in a strap; the wrapping meant order.

column3: Alone it appears in 我妹, as an address to a younger girl, and in compounds: 姐妹 (sisters), 学妹 (a female junior at school). 妹妹 is the everyday word.
column7: My younger sister is ten this year.
column9: Alone it appears in 我妹, as an address to a younger girl, and in compounds: 姐妹 (sisters), 學妹 (a female junior at school). 妹妹 is the everyday word.

column3: With a light second syllable: mèimei. It is also how you call a girl younger than you, relative or not. The plural idea is 姐妹, with the older sister first.
column9: With a light second syllable: mèimei. It is also how you call a girl younger than you, relative or not. The plural idea is 姐妹, with the older sister first.

column3: It is the father's mother. The mother's mother is 外婆, or 姥姥 in the north. Children also call an old woman among the neighbors 奶奶, as a respectful "granny".
column7: My grandmother is seventy this year.
column9: It is the father's mother. The mother's mother is 外婆, or 姥姥 in the north. Children also call an old woman among the neighbors 奶奶, as a respectful "granny".

column3: It is the father's father, with a light second syllable. The mother's father is 外公, or 姥爷 in the north. 老爷爷 is a respectful "grandpa" for an old man you don't know.
column7: Grandpa is watching TV at home.
column9: It is the father's father, with a light second syllable. The mother's father is 外公, or 姥爺 in the north. 老爺爺 is a respectful "grandpa" for an old man you don't know.

column3: The 子 is light. Its partner is 女儿 (daughter); 儿女 means sons and daughters together. 儿 began as a picture of an infant whose skull has not yet closed.
column9: The 子 is light. Its partner is 女兒 (daughter); 兒女 means sons and daughters together. 兒 began as a picture of an infant whose skull has not yet closed.

column3: Daughter: 女 (female) plus 儿 (child). In pinyin an apostrophe splits the syllables so they do not run together: nǚ'ér.
column9: Daughter: 女 (female) plus 兒 (child). In pinyin an apostrophe splits the syllables so they do not run together: nǚ'ér.

column3: The usual word for a child, and for one's own children at any age: 你有孩子吗？ The plural is 孩子们. 小孩 is a close everyday synonym.
column9: The usual word for a child, and for one's own children at any age: 你有孩子嗎？ The plural is 孩子們. 小孩 is a close everyday synonym.

column3: A light noun ending: 桌子, 房子, 杯子, 椅子. It adds no meaning, and the noun is not said without it.
column6: Zhè ge bēi zi hěn dà.
column9: A light noun ending: 桌子, 房子, 杯子, 椅子. It adds no meaning, and the noun is not said without it.

column3: Your relatives, usually the close ones, as against friends: 家人和朋友. 都是一家人 means "we are all family". The pig 豕 under the roof is a later corruption of an older sound part, so "a roof over a pig" is a folk etymology.
column9: Your relatives, usually the close ones, as against friends: 家人和朋友. 都是一家人 means "we are all family". The pig 豕 under the roof is a later corruption of an older sound part, so "a roof over a pig" is a folk etymology.

column3: Before a noun it needs a measure word: 这个人, 这本书. It points near; 那 points far. 这 was first a verb meaning "to meet", read yàn, and was later borrowed for "this".
column9: Before a noun it needs a measure word: 這個人, 這本書. It points near; 那 points far. 這 was first a verb meaning "to meet", read yàn, and was later borrowed for "this".

column3: The far partner of 这, with the same need for a measure word: 那个人. At the start of a sentence it means "in that case": 那你去吧. It was first the name of a state, and later borrowed for "that".
column9: The far partner of 這, with the same need for a measure word: 那個人. At the start of a sentence it means "in that case": 那你去吧. It was first the name of a state, and later borrowed for "that".

column3: The northern spoken form of 这里: 来这儿, 坐这儿吧. In Taiwan and the south 这里 is what people say in speech too. Here 儿 is not a syllable of its own but a suffix that only gives the syllable an r.
column9: The northern spoken form of 這裡: 來這兒, 坐這兒吧. In Taiwan and the south 這裡 is what people say in speech too. Here 兒 is not a syllable of its own but a suffix that only gives the syllable an r.

column3: The far partner of 这儿: 在那儿, 去那儿, 我的书在那儿. That is northern speech; in Taiwan and the south 那里 is the everyday spoken form. 那 was first the name of a state, and later borrowed for "that".
column9: The far partner of 這兒: 在那兒, 去那兒, 我的書在那兒. That is northern speech; in Taiwan and the south 那裡 is the everyday spoken form. 那 was first the name of a state, and later borrowed for "that".

column3: It is as spoken as 这儿 and fits writing too, so it is the safe choice: 请在这里等我, and on signs, 这里禁止吸烟. The 里 is light: zhèli. Its partners are 那里 and 哪里. 里 is a field 田 on earth 土: an old measure of land, and so a place.
column9: It is as spoken as 這兒 and fits writing too, so it is the safe choice: 請在這裡等我, and on signs, 這裡禁止吸煙. The 裡 is light: zhèli. Its partners are 那裡 and 哪裡. 裡 is a field 田 on earth 土: an old measure of land, and so a place.

column3: It is the more formal match of 那儿, for a place away from both of you: 那里有一家商店. The 里 is light and means no "inside" here: nàli. 那 was first the name of a state, and later borrowed for "that".
column7: There is a shop over there.
column9: It is the more formal match of 那兒, for a place away from both of you: 那裡有一家商店. The 裡 is light and means no "inside" here: nàli. 那 was first the name of a state, and later borrowed for "that".

column3: It is already plural, so the noun follows with no 个: 这些书, 这些人. Alone it is a pronoun: 这些是我的. For one thing, say 这个.
column6: Zhèxiē shū dōu shì xīn de.
column9: It is already plural, so the noun follows with no 個: 這些書, 這些人. Alone it is a pronoun: 這些是我的. For one thing, say 這個.

column3: It is the plural of 那个, so no 个 follows: 那些人, 那些书. Alone it is a pronoun: 那些是我的衣服. Its near partner is 这些.
column9: It is the plural of 那個, so no 個 follows: 那些人, 那些書. Alone it is a pronoun: 那些是我的衣服. Its near partner is 這些.

column3: It means this side or here, with a sense of direction: 这边请 is "this way, please". 我这边 is "my end", as in a phone call. Its partners are 那边 and 哪边. The walking part 辶 was added to 边 in the bronze inscriptions.
column9: It means this side or here, with a sense of direction: 這邊請 is "this way, please". 我這邊 is "my end", as in a phone call. Its partners are 那邊 and 哪邊. The walking part 辶 was added to 邊 in the bronze inscriptions.

column3: It means over there, set against 这边: 这边是学校，那边是商店. The 边 is light: nàbian. 你那边 is "your end", as in a phone call.
column7: There is a station over there.
column9: It means over there, set against 這邊: 這邊是學校，那邊是商店. The 邊 is light: nàbian. 你那邊 is "your end", as in a phone call.

column3: What. The question word stays where the answer would go: 你吃什么？ ("you eat what?"). Before a noun it asks "what kind": 什么书？
column7: What do you want to eat?
column9: What. The question word stays where the answer would go: 你吃什麼？ ("you eat what?"). Before a noun it asks "what kind": 什麼書？

column3: With 都 or 也 it turns into everyone or no one: 谁都知道, 谁也不知道. 谁的 asks whose: 这是谁的书？
column9: With 都 or 也 it turns into everyone or no one: 誰都知道, 誰也不知道. 誰的 asks whose: 這是誰的書？

column3: It goes before a measure word: 哪个, 哪本书. With 都 it means any: 哪个都行. Before the 20th century it was written as 那.
column9: It goes before a measure word: 哪個, 哪本書. With 都 it means any: 哪個都行. Before the 20th century it was written as 那.

column3: The northern spoken "where": 你去哪儿？ With 都 it means anywhere: 哪儿都行. 哪儿的话 means "not at all". In Taiwan and the south 哪里 is the everyday word. Before the 20th century 哪 was written as 那.
column9: The northern spoken "where": 你去哪兒？ With 都 it means anywhere: 哪兒都行. 哪兒的話 means "not at all". In Taiwan and the south 哪裡 is the everyday word. Before the 20th century 哪 was written as 那.

column3: It is the more formal match of 哪儿. As a reply to praise, 哪里 or 哪里哪里 means "not at all", a modest denial. It can also mean anywhere or nowhere: 哪里都有.
column9: It is the more formal match of 哪兒. As a reply to praise, 哪裡 or 哪裡哪裡 means "not at all", a modest denial. It can also mean anywhere or nowhere: 哪裡都有.

column3: The plural of 哪个, with no 个 before the noun: 哪些书？ In 有哪些人？ it asks for the whole list, "who all is there". For one thing, say 哪个.
column9: The plural of 哪個, with no 個 before the noun: 哪些書？ In 有哪些人？ it asks for the whole list, "who all is there". For one thing, say 哪個.

column3: Before a verb it asks how: 怎么走, 怎么做. With a negative or surprise it asks why: 你怎么不去？ 你怎么了？ asks what is wrong. 怎么样 asks "how is it?". 怎 is first recorded around the 10th century, in 怎生, and may be a contraction of "to do what".
column7: How do I get to the airport?
column9: Before a verb it asks how: 怎麼走, 怎麼做. With a negative or surprise it asks why: 你怎麼不去？ 你怎麼了？ asks what is wrong. 怎麼樣 asks "how is it?". 怎 is first recorded around the 10th century, in 怎生, and may be a contraction of "to do what".

column3: It is spoken, and asks both what someone is doing and what for: 你在干什么？ Said sharply, 你干什么！ means "what do you think you're doing?". This 干 is read gàn, "to do"; read gān it is "dry".
column9: It is spoken, and asks both what someone is doing and what for: 你在幹什麼？ Said sharply, 你幹什麼！ means "what do you think you're doing?". This 幹 is read gàn, "to do"; read gān it is "dry".

column3: It asks a question that expects yes: 你是不是累了？ It is a verb-not-verb question, so it takes no 吗. At the end of a statement it checks it: 他是老师，是不是？ The 不 in the middle began as a picture of a flower's calyx.
column9: It asks a question that expects yes: 你是不是累了？ It is a verb-not-verb question, so it takes no 嗎. At the end of a statement it checks it: 他是老師，是不是？ The 不 in the middle began as a picture of a flower's calyx.

column3: It links two nouns: 我是学生. It is not used before an adjective: say 我很高兴, not 我是高兴. In 是…的 it stresses a detail: 我是昨天来的. 是 alone answers "yes" to an is-question. Its sense "to be" is a late one, from the Eastern Han dynasty.
column9: It links two nouns: 我是學生. It is not used before an adjective: say 我很高興, not 我是高興. In 是…的 it stresses a detail: 我是昨天來的. 是 alone answers "yes" to an is-question. Its sense "to be" is a late one, from the Eastern Han dynasty.

column3: To have and "there is": 我有一本书; 桌子上有一本书. Its negative is 没有, never 不有. Its hand, once written 又 (yòu), gives the sound, and its 月 is a changed 肉 "meat".
column6: Wǒ jiā yǒu sì kǒu rén.
column7: There are four people in my family.
column9: To have and "there is": 我有一本書; 桌子上有一本書. Its negative is 沒有, never 不有. Its hand, once written 又 (yòu), gives the sound, and its 月 is a changed 肉 "meat".

column3: Before a verb it gives the place of the action (我在学校学习) or marks it in progress (他在吃饭). As a verb it answers "is he in?": 他在吗？ 不在 means "not here". The 土 at the bottom is a later corruption of 士, which was only a sound part.
column9: Before a verb it gives the place of the action (我在學校學習) or marks it in progress (他在吃飯). As a verb it answers "is he in?": 他在嗎？ 不在 means "not here". The 土 at the bottom is a later corruption of 士, which was only a sound part.

column3: It negates habits, wishes and what will happen: 我不去; 没 negates the past. Before another fourth tone it is said bú (不是 is bú shì), though dictionaries write bù. It began as a picture of a flower's calyx.
column9: It negates habits, wishes and what will happen: 我不去; 沒 negates the past. Before another fourth tone it is said bú (不是 is bú shì), though dictionaries write bù. It began as a picture of a flower's calyx.

column3: It negates 有 and what already happened: 我没吃, 我没有书. At the end, 吃了没有？ asks "have you eaten?". 不 negates habits and wishes instead. This 没 may be a colloquial variant of 勿 or 未 that mixed with 有, rather than the mò "drown" word.
column9: It negates 有 and what already happened: 我沒吃, 我沒有書. At the end, 吃了沒有？ asks "have you eaten?". 不 negates habits and wishes instead. This 沒 may be a colloquial variant of 勿 or 未 that mixed with 有, rather than the mò "drown" word.

column3: Does not have, "there is no", and the negative of past actions: 他没有来 ("he did not come"). At the end of a question it asks "did you or not": 你吃了没有？
column7: I don't have an older brother.
column9: Does not have, "there is no", and the negative of past actions: 他沒有來 ("he did not come"). At the end of a question it asks "did you or not": 你吃了沒有？

column3: It agrees: 你说得对. It also means toward or about: 他对我很好, 对中文有兴趣. 对不对？ and 对吧？ ask "right?". The opposite is 错. Its original meaning is unclear, perhaps "to develop land"; it was later borrowed for "to reply".
column6: Zhè ge zì duì bu duì?
column9: It agrees: 你說得對. It also means toward or about: 他對我很好, 對中文有興趣. 對不對？ and 對吧？ ask "right?". The opposite is 錯. Its original meaning is unclear, perhaps "to develop land"; it was later borrowed for "to reply".

column3: It follows a verb to say it went wrong: 写错, 说错, 走错. 没错 means "that's right" and 不错 means "not bad", even good. The opposite is 对. Besides "wrong" it has senses such as "whetstone" and "criss-cross, interlocking".
column9: It follows a verb to say it went wrong: 寫錯, 說錯, 走錯. 沒錯 means "that's right" and 不錯 means "not bad", even good. The opposite is 對. Besides "wrong" it has senses such as "whetstone" and "criss-cross, interlocking".

column3: Said alone, 不对！ stops someone: that is wrong. It also says something is off, not only incorrect: 声音不对 is a sound that seems odd. Before a fourth tone 不 is said bú. 不 began as a picture of a flower's calyx; its sense of no came back to it from 否.
column9: Said alone, 不對！ stops someone: that is wrong. It also says something is off, not only incorrect: 聲音不對 is a sound that seems odd. Before a fourth tone 不 is said bú. 不 began as a picture of a flower's calyx; its sense of no came back to it from 否.

column3: Beside a size word it means not big (房间不大), but before other adjectives it softens: 不大好 is not very good. 不太 is used the same way. 大 is a standing person facing forward, and the old forms do not show outstretched arms.
column9: Beside a size word it means not big (房間不大), but before other adjectives it softens: 不大好 is not very good. 不太 is used the same way. 大 is a standing person facing forward, and the old forms do not show outstretched arms.

column3: It means no need, not don't use: 不用买 is no need to buy; to forbid, say 别买. As a reply to thanks, 不用谢, and to an offer, 不用，谢谢. 用 is 同 with a handle added.
column9: It means no need, not don't use: 不用買 is no need to buy; to forbid, say 別買. As a reply to thanks, 不用謝, and to an offer, 不用，謝謝. 用 is 同 with a handle added.

column3: It goes between the subject and the verb, never at the end the way English puts too: 我也是学生. With 都 the order is 也都. In 一…也不 it means even: 他一口也没吃. One theory sees in 也 a child with its mouth open, crying.
column9: It goes between the subject and the verb, never at the end the way English puts too: 我也是學生. With 都 the order is 也都. In 一…也不 it means even: 他一口也沒吃. One theory sees in 也 a child with its mouth open, crying.

column3: It follows the group it covers and comes before the verb: 我们都是学生. Before a time or number it means already: 都十点了.
column9: It follows the group it covers and comes before the verb: 我們都是學生. Before a time or number it means already: 都十點了.

column3: Before an adjective it often only fills the slot and means little more than is: 她很高. Bare 她高 sounds like a comparison. For real emphasis, stress 很 or use 非常. 很 first meant to disobey or defy, and has meant very since the Yuan dynasty.
column9: Before an adjective it often only fills the slot and means little more than is: 她很高. Bare 她高 sounds like a comparison. For real emphasis, stress 很 or use 非常. 很 first meant to disobey or defy, and has meant very since the Yuan dynasty.

column3: Usually with 了 at the end: 太贵了 is too expensive, but 太好了！ is great! 不太 means not very: 不太贵 is not very expensive. 太 is 大 with a dot added, so 大 has no dot.
column9: Usually with 了 at the end: 太貴了 is too expensive, but 太好了！ is great! 不太 means not very: 不太貴 is not very expensive. 太 is 大 with a dot added, so 大 has no dot.

column3: Unlike 很, it is never a mere filler: it always means very, and it also goes before verbs of feeling (非常喜欢). As an adjective it means unusual: 非常时期 is an extraordinary time. 常 first meant a skirt-like lower garment and was borrowed for long-lasting or often.
column9: Unlike 很, it is never a mere filler: it always means very, and it also goes before verbs of feeling (非常喜歡). As an adjective it means unusual: 非常時期 is an extraordinary time. 常 first meant a skirt-like lower garment and was borrowed for long-lasting or often.

column3: Before an adjective it carries feeling: 这个字真难写 is this character is so hard to write, where 很难写 would only state it. It also means real: 真人, 真话. Some scholars read an oracle-bone form made of a spoon 匕 and 鼎 as an early 真.
column6: Zhè ge zì zhēn nán xiě.
column7: This character is really hard to write.
column9: Before an adjective it carries feeling: 這個字真難寫 is this character is so hard to write, where 很難寫 would only state it. It also means real: 真人, 真話. Some scholars read an oracle-bone form made of a spoon 匕 and 鼎 as an early 真.

column3: As a question, 真的吗？ is really? and a reply of 真的 is yes, really. In a statement it stresses sincerity: 我真的不知道. Before a noun it means real: 真的钱 is real money. 的 began as 旳, meaning bright.
column9: As a question, 真的嗎？ is really? and a reply of 真的 is yes, really. In a statement it stresses sincerity: 我真的不知道. Before a noun it means real: 真的錢 is real money. 的 began as 旳, meaning bright.

column3: As an answer, OK, will do: 行，没问题. 行吗？ asks permission, 不行 refuses, and 他很行 means he is capable. 行 began as a picture of a street crossing.
column7: Is it OK to go today?
column9: As an answer, OK, will do: 行，沒問題. 行嗎？ asks permission, 不行 refuses, and 他很行 means he is capable. 行 began as a picture of a street crossing.

column3: 好朋友 is a close friend, and 交朋友 is to make friends. The last syllable is light on the mainland (péngyou); in Taiwan it is usually a full third tone, péngyǒu. 朋 began as two strings with cowries attached, and the shape was later corrupted into a double 月.
column6: Tā shì wǒ de hǎo péngyou.
column9: 好朋友 is a close friend, and 交朋友 is to make friends. The last syllable is light on the mainland (péngyou); in Taiwan it is usually a full third tone, péngyǒu. 朋 began as two strings with cowries attached, and the shape was later corrupted into a double 月.

column3: A fixed word for a partner, not just a male friend; that is 男性朋友. Without 的 it is natural: 我男朋友. 男友 is the short form, and 前男友 is an ex.
column9: A fixed word for a partner, not just a male friend; that is 男性朋友. Without 的 it is natural: 我男朋友. 男友 is the short form, and 前男友 is an ex.

column3: A fixed word for a partner, not just a female friend; that is 女性朋友. Without 的 it is natural: 我女朋友. 女友 is the short form, and 前女友 is an ex. 女 shows a woman with folded arms, kneeling or standing.
column9: A fixed word for a partner, not just a female friend; that is 女性朋友. Without 的 it is natural: 我女朋友. 女友 is the short form, and 前女友 is an ex. 女 shows a woman with folded arms, kneeling or standing.

column3: Literally little friend: what a teacher or adult calls a child, 小朋友，你几岁了？ A group is 小朋友们. In Taiwan, parents also use it for their own child.
column7: Little one, how old are you?
column9: Literally little friend: what a teacher or adult calls a child, 小朋友，你幾歲了？ A group is 小朋友們. In Taiwan, parents also use it for their own child.

column3: A boy, a male student or any young guy: 我们班有十个男生. In Taiwan it is also the ordinary word for a man or boy in general. 男人 stresses an adult man.
column6: Wǒmen bān yǒu shí ge nánshēng.
column9: A boy, a male student or any young guy: 我們班有十個男生. In Taiwan it is also the ordinary word for a man or boy in general. 男人 stresses an adult man.

column3: A girl, a female student or any young woman. In Taiwan it is also the ordinary word for a girl or woman in general. 女孩 is girl, and 女人 stresses an adult woman.
column6: Nàge nǚshēng shì wǒ de tóngxué.
column9: A girl, a female student or any young woman. In Taiwan it is also the ordinary word for a girl or woman in general. 女孩 is girl, and 女人 stresses an adult woman.

column3: A grown man; it can also mean a woman's husband or man, as in 她的男人, which is informal. For a boy or male student, 男生.
column9: A grown man; it can also mean a woman's husband or man, as in 她的男人, which is informal. For a boy or male student, 男生.

column3: A plain description of an adult woman, not a way to address her; for that use 小姐, 女士, the name or a title. In speech it can also mean wife: 他的女人. 女 shows a woman with folded arms, kneeling or standing.
column9: A plain description of an adult woman, not a way to address her; for that use 小姐, 女士, the name or a title. In speech it can also mean wife: 他的女人. 女 shows a woman with folded arms, kneeling or standing.

column3: The 儿 ending is a northern mainland speech habit; Taiwan and the south simply say 男孩. Both mean the same, and 男孩 is the form for writing. One scholar groups 孩 in a word family meaning root, germ, generative core.
column9: The 兒 ending is a northern mainland speech habit; Taiwan and the south simply say 男孩. Both mean the same, and 男孩 is the form for writing. One scholar groups 孩 in a word family meaning root, germ, generative core.

column3: Add 小 for a little girl: 小女孩儿. A girl in general is 女孩, and 女儿 means daughter, not girl. The 儿 form is mainly northern mainland speech. 儿's older form pictures an infant with a soft spot in the skull.
column6: Tā shì yī ge xiǎo nǚháir.
column9: Add 小 for a little girl: 小女孩兒. A girl in general is 女孩, and 女兒 means daughter, not girl. The 兒 form is mainly northern mainland speech. 兒's older form pictures an infant with a soft spot in the skull.

column3: Said to an adult, it means grow up: 你不是小孩儿了. 小孩子 and 小孩 are the same word; the 儿 form is mainly northern mainland speech. The 儿 at the end is the diminutive ending, said as a final r.
column7: You are not a little kid anymore.
column9: Said to an adult, it means grow up: 你不是小孩兒了. 小孩子 and 小孩 are the same word; the 兒 form is mainly northern mainland speech. The 兒 at the end is the diminutive ending, said as a final r.

column3: The elderly in general; 家里有老人 means there are elderly relatives, often parents or grandparents. To address one respectfully, say 老人家, not 老人.
column6: Nà wèi lǎorén shì wǒ de línjū.
column7: That elderly man is my neighbor.
column9: The elderly in general; 家裡有老人 means there are elderly relatives, often parents or grandparents. To address one respectfully, say 老人家, not 老人.

column3: A fixed word, not little older sister. The second syllable is light on the mainland (xiǎojie) but a full third tone in Taiwan (xiǎojiě). In Taiwan 王小姐 is an everyday polite title; on the mainland the slang sense makes it risky, so 女士 is safer.
column9: A fixed word, not little older sister. The second syllable is light on the mainland (xiǎojie) but a full third tone in Taiwan (xiǎojiě). In Taiwan 王小姐 is an everyday polite title; on the mainland the slang sense makes it risky, so 女士 is safer.

column3: Literally born earlier. After a surname it is Mr., as in 王先生, and a wife can say 我先生 for my husband. The 生 is light on the mainland (xiānsheng) but usually a full tone in Taiwan (xiānshēng).
column9: Literally born earlier. After a surname it is Mr., as in 王先生, and a wife can say 我先生 for my husband. The 生 is light on the mainland (xiānsheng) but usually a full tone in Taiwan (xiānshēng).

column3: Both the job and the way to address one: 老师好！ or 王老师. The more formal word for the profession is 教师.
column9: Both the job and the way to address one: 老師好！ or 王老師. The more formal word for the profession is 教師.

column3: Classmate, fellow student. Teachers also use it to address students: 同学们好！ 同 means "same" and 学 means "study". The bottom of 学 is 子 (child).
column9: Classmate, fellow student. Teachers also use it to address students: 同學們好！ 同 means "same" and 學 means "study". The bottom of 學 is 子 (child).

column3: The person: 看医生 is to see a doctor, with 看, not 见. After a surname, 王医生 is Dr. Wang. 医师 is the formal title.
column7: I'm going to see the doctor tomorrow.
column9: The person: 看醫生 is to see a doctor, with 看, not 見. After a surname, 王醫生 is Dr. Wang. 醫師 is the formal title.

column3: Manual or factory work: 建筑工人 is a construction worker. Not for office staff, who are 职员; 工作人员 means staff in any job. 工 is the same word as 功 (merit) and 攻 (attack).
column9: Manual or factory work: 建築工人 is a construction worker. Not for office staff, who are 職員; 工作人員 means staff in any job. 工 is the same word as 功 (merit) and 攻 (attack).

column3: Both a sick person and a patient in care. 患者 is the formal word in medical writing, while 病人 is what people say. 看病 is to see a doctor.
column6: Yīyuàn lǐ yǒu hěn duō bìngrén.
column7: There are a lot of patients in the hospital.
column9: Both a sick person and a patient in care. 患者 is the formal word in medical writing, while 病人 is what people say. 看病 is to see a doctor.

column3: Someone you know through the internet, even if you have since met in person: 我昨天和网友见面了. Also anyone posting online, "netizens": 网友们的看法不同. 网 (net) plus 友 (friend).
column9: Someone you know through the internet, even if you have since met in person: 我昨天和網友見面了. Also anyone posting online, "netizens": 網友們的看法不同. 網 (net) plus 友 (friend).

column3: Everyone except you or me: 别人都走了 is all the others left. Mainland speech often makes 人 light (biéren), while Taiwan says biérén. 别 before a verb is don't, as in 别说; here it means other. 别 began as a knife cutting flesh from bone.
column9: Everyone except you or me: 別人都走了 is all the others left. Mainland speech often makes 人 light (biéren), while Taiwan says biérén. 別 before a verb is don't, as in 別說; here it means other. 別 began as a knife cutting flesh from bone.

column3: It counts years with no measure word: 三年. A calendar year is read digit by digit: 二〇二五年. For a person's age, use 岁, not 年. 年 first meant harvest and came to mean year; its parts were 禾, grain, and a sound.
column6: Wǒ xué le liǎng nián Hànyǔ.
column7: I have studied Chinese for two years.
column9: It counts years with no measure word: 三年. A calendar year is read digit by digit: 二〇二五年. For a person's age, use 歲, not 年. 年 first meant harvest and came to mean year; its parts were 禾, grain, and a sound.

column3: Month names are number plus 月: 三月 is March, no 个. To count months, add 个: 两个月. In speech the moon is usually 月亮. In 有 the 月 is meat, and in 前 it is a boat, not a moon.
column9: Month names are number plus 月: 三月 is March, no 個. To count months, add 個: 兩個月. In speech the moon is usually 月亮. In 有 the 月 is meat, and in 前 it is a boat, not a moon.

column3: Day and "sun". In dates the written form is 日 (三月五日) and speech says 号 (五号). It is a picture of the sun; the stroke in the middle was added to keep it apart from 口.
column4: 十月十三日是我的生日。
column5: 十月十三日是我的生日。
column6: Shíyuè shísān rì shì wǒ de shēngrì.
column9: Day and "sun". In dates the written form is 日 (三月五日) and speech says 號 (五號). It is a picture of the sun; the stroke in the middle was added to keep it apart from 口.

column3: It says the date in speech: 五号, where writing prefers 日. After a number it also numbers things: 三号房间 is room 3, and 大号 is a large size. 号 goes back to a roaring tiger with a line for the breath, and 口 was added later.
column9: It says the date in speech: 五號, where writing prefers 日. After a number it also numbers things: 三號房間 is room 3, and 大號 is a large size. 號 goes back to a roaring tiger with a line for the breath, and 口 was added later.

column3: It counts days with no measure word: 三天. It is also the sky (蓝天) and the weather (天气). In oracle-bone writing, 天 is a standing man 大 with a head drawn in four variants.
column6: Yī tiān yǒu èrshísì ge xiǎoshí.
column9: It counts days with no measure word: 三天. It is also the sky (藍天) and the weather (天氣). In oracle-bone writing, 天 is a standing man 大 with a head drawn in four variants.

column3: Time words sit before the verb or before the subject: 今天我不忙. It can also mean nowadays: 今天的中国. One theory is that 今 shows something held in the mouth.
column9: Time words sit before the verb or before the subject: 今天我不忙. It can also mean nowadays: 今天的中國. One theory is that 今 shows something held in the mouth.

column3: 明天见！ is a common way of parting. It can also mean the future: 美好的明天 is a bright tomorrow. 明 pictures dawn: the sun just rising while the moon has not yet set.
column9: 明天見！ is a common way of parting. It can also mean the future: 美好的明天 is a bright tomorrow. 明 pictures dawn: the sun just rising while the moon has not yet set.

column3: It goes before the verb: 昨天我没去学校. Last night is 昨天晚上 or 昨晚. 昨 is related to 昔, a word for the past.
column7: I didn't go to school yesterday.
column9: It goes before the verb: 昨天我沒去學校. Last night is 昨天晚上 or 昨晚. 昨 is related to 昔, a word for the past.

column3: The day after tomorrow. Here 后 is "after". The row runs 前天, 昨天, 今天, 明天, 后天.
column7: The day after tomorrow is Saturday.
column9: The day after tomorrow. Here 後 is "after". The row runs 前天, 昨天, 今天, 明天, 後天.

column3: Two days ago. Going back one more, 大前天 is three days ago; the day after tomorrow is 后天. The 月 in 前 is a worn-down boat: it began as a foot on a boat moving forward.
column7: The day before yesterday I was at home.
column9: Two days ago. Going back one more, 大前天 is three days ago; the day after tomorrow is 後天. The 月 in 前 is a worn-down boat: it began as a foot on a boat moving forward.

column3: Like 去年 and 明年, it sits before the verb with no 在: 今年我学汉语. 前年 and 后年 are the years before last and after next.
column9: Like 去年 and 明年, it sits before the verb with no 在: 今年我學漢語. 前年 and 後年 are the years before last and after next.

column3: It sits before the verb or the subject: 明年我想去中国. 后年 is the year after next, as 后天 is the day after tomorrow.
column7: Next year I want to go to China.
column9: It sits before the verb or the subject: 明年我想去中國. 後年 is the year after next, as 後天 is the day after tomorrow.

column3: Last year. 去 elsewhere means "go", but here it means "gone by": 去年 is not "go year".
column7: Last year I lived in Beijing.
column9: Last year. 去 elsewhere means "go", but here it means "gone by": 去年 is not "go year".

column3: Days are numbered: 星期一 is Monday. Sunday is 星期天 or 星期日, never 星期七. 周一 is the shorter form of 星期一. The 日 in 星 is 晶, glossed twinkling stars, simplified into 日.
column7: What day of the week is it?
column9: Days are numbered: 星期一 is Monday. Sunday is 星期天 or 星期日, never 星期七. 週一 is the shorter form of 星期一. The 日 in 星 is 晶, glossed twinkling stars, simplified into 日.

column3: Sunday, the one day without a number. It is the same as 星期天, and 星期日 reads a little more formal, as on calendars and timetables. 周日 is shorter.
column7: We don't have class on Sunday.
column9: Sunday, the one day without a number. It is the same as 星期天, and 星期日 reads a little more formal, as on calendars and timetables. 週日 is shorter.

column3: The everyday word for Sunday; 星期日 is what calendars print. To ask the day, use 星期几: 今天星期几？ 期 once had the sun 日 as its part, which was later changed to the moon 月.
column7: Where do you want to go on Sunday?
column9: The everyday word for Sunday; 星期日 is what calendars print. To ask the day, use 星期幾: 今天星期幾？ 期 once had the sun 日 as its part, which was later changed to the moon 月.

column3: 过生日 is the usual verb for celebrating one: 他明天过生日. The greeting is 生日快乐. 生 has derivatives such as 性 and 姓.
column9: 過生日 is the usual verb for celebrating one: 他明天過生日. The greeting is 生日快樂. 生 has derivatives such as 性 and 姓.

column3: The date as a whole, as on a form: 请写日期. For the day of the month alone, say 号 or 日 (五号); for the time of day, 时间. 期 is the word for a stipulated time.
column9: The date as a whole, as on a form: 請寫日期. For the day of the month alone, say 號 or 日 (五號); for the time of day, 時間. 期 is the word for a stipulated time.

column3: 年 and 天 take no measure word, so 半年 and 半天, not 半个年; months and hours do: 半个月. After the unit it means and a half: 一年半 is a year and a half. 半 is 八, to divide, with 牛: a cow cut into two halves.
column7: I studied Chinese for half a year.
column9: 年 and 天 take no measure word, so 半年 and 半天, not 半個年; months and hours do: 半個月. After the unit it means and a half: 一年半 is a year and a half. 半 is 八, to divide, with 牛: a cow cut into two halves.

column3: Half a day, but often ages: 我等了半天 is I waited ages, usually with a note of complaint. No 个 is needed.
column7: I waited for you for ages.
column9: Half a day, but often ages: 我等了半天 is I waited ages, usually with a note of complaint. No 個 is needed.

column3: The greeting is 新年快乐. For Chinese New Year, people say 春节 or 过年; 新年 is the turn of the calendar year, though the greeting is said at both. 新 began as chopping wood, the original of 薪 firewood, and was borrowed for new.
column9: The greeting is 新年快樂. For Chinese New Year, people say 春節 or 過年; 新年 is the turn of the calendar year, though the greeting is said at both. 新 began as chopping wood, the original of 薪 firewood, and was borrowed for new.

column3: Early, and "morning": 早 is also the greeting "morning!". 早 before a verb says early: 早睡 "go to bed early". It started as a picture of an acorn. As a way to remember (not history): the sun 日 just above the horizon.
column6: Nǐ jīntiān qǐ de zhēn zǎo.
column7: You got up really early today.
column9: Early, and "morning": 早 is also the greeting "morning!". 早 before a verb says early: 早睡 "go to bed early". It started as a picture of an acorn. As a way to remember (not history): the sun 日 just above the horizon.

column3: Morning. Light 上: zǎoshang. Put the time before the verb and the clock time after: 早上七点. 早上好 is the greeting.
column7: I get up at seven in the morning.
column9: Morning. Light 上: zǎoshang. Put the time before the verb and the clock time after: 早上七點. 早上好 is the greeting.

column3: The morning hours up to noon, before the clock time: 上午九点. 早上 is the early part of it; the pair is 下午. 午 is a pestle and unrelated to 干.
column7: I have class in the morning.
column9: The morning hours up to noon, before the clock time: 上午九點. 早上 is the early part of it; the pair is 下午. 午 is a pestle and unrelated to 干.

column3: The hours around noon and lunch: 中午吃饭. Don't use 午 alone for noon; say 中午, or 正午 for exactly twelve.
column9: The hours around noon and lunch: 中午吃飯. Don't use 午 alone for noon; say 中午, or 正午 for exactly twelve.

column3: It comes before the time or the verb: 下午三点, 下午去商店. The morning is 上午, and 中午 is noon. 午 began as a picture of a pestle and has nothing to do with 干.
column7: I'm going to the shop this afternoon.
column9: It comes before the time or the verb: 下午三點, 下午去商店. The morning is 上午, and 中午 is noon. 午 began as a picture of a pestle and has nothing to do with 干.

column3: It means late as well as evening: 太晚了 is "too late", 来晚了 "arrived late", and 晚 starts 晚饭 and 晚安.
column9: It means late as well as evening: 太晚了 is "too late", 來晚了 "arrived late", and 晚 starts 晚飯 and 晚安.

column3: It covers evening and the night before bed, so 晚上十点 is fine; 晚上好 greets someone in the evening.
column7: I watch TV in the evening.
column9: It covers evening and the night before bed, so 晚上十點 is fine; 晚上好 greets someone in the evening.

column3: Daytime, set against 晚上: 白天上班，晚上休息. It is a time word that goes before the verb with no 在. For 白 there are two theories: a picture of an acorn, or a human head.
column9: Daytime, set against 晚上: 白天上班，晚上休息. It is a time word that goes before the verb with no 在. For 白 there are two theories: a picture of an acorn, or a human head.

column3: It can come before or after the subject: 现在我很忙 or 我现在很忙. For "just now" use 刚才 instead. 现 is a stative form of the verb "to see", meaning "to be visible; to appear".
column9: It can come before or after the subject: 現在我很忙 or 我現在很忙. For "just now" use 剛才 instead. 現 is a stative form of the verb "to see", meaning "to be visible; to appear".

column3: After a clause with 的 it means "when": 吃饭的时候. 什么时候 asks "when". The 候 is light on the mainland (shíhou); in Taiwan it is shíhòu.
column9: After a clause with 的 it means "when": 吃飯的時候. 什麼時候 asks "when". The 候 is light on the mainland (shíhou); in Taiwan it is shíhòu.

column3: Time as an amount or period: 有时间, 没时间, 时间不够. For a clock time say 点 instead: 三点. Here 间 is read jiān, as in "between"; read jiàn it means "gap" or "to separate".
column9: Time as an amount or period: 有時間, 沒時間, 時間不夠. For a clock time say 點 instead: 三點. Here 間 is read jiān, as in "between"; read jiàn it means "gap" or "to separate".

column3: Hour as a length of time: 一个小时, 两个小时. A clock hour is 点, not 小时. 时 has 日 (sun) as meaning part. Half an hour is 半个小时, and 钟头 is a spoken synonym.
column6: Wǒ xué le liǎng ge xiǎoshí.
column9: Hour as a length of time: 一個小時, 兩個小時. A clock hour is 點, not 小時. 時 has 日 (sun) as meaning part. Half an hour is 半個小時, and 鐘頭 is a spoken synonym.

column3: A short while: 等一会儿, and 一会儿见 means "see you in a bit". Its 会 is not the "can" verb. It is said huìr. Here 儿 is not the word "child" but only the r sound added to the end.
column9: A short while: 等一會兒, and 一會兒見 means "see you in a bit". Its 會 is not the "can" verb. It is said huìr. Here 兒 is not the word "child" but only the r sound added to the end.

column3: It goes before the verb or opens the sentence: 有时候我坐车. 有时 is a shorter, more written form; 常常 is "often", a step up.
column9: It goes before the verb or opens the sentence: 有時候我坐車. 有時 is a shorter, more written form; 常常 is "often", a step up.

column3: A shorter, slightly more written form of 有时候, often paired for contrast: 有时…有时…, as in the example. A folk story says 有 is a hand holding meat, but the oldest script shows no meat.
column6: Wǒ yǒushí zuò chē, yǒushí zǒulù.
column7: I sometimes take a bus and sometimes walk.
column9: A shorter, slightly more written form of 有時候, often paired for contrast: 有時…有時…, as in the example. A folk story says 有 is a hand holding meat, but the oldest script shows no meat.

column3: It looks to the near future: 我马上来. 就 adds urgency: 马上就到 "arriving any moment". It can look back too: 他马上就走了 "he left right away". 马 began as a picture of a horse facing left, its mane flowing in the wind.
column6: Nǐ děng yīxià, wǒ mǎshàng lái.
column7: Wait a moment, I'll be right there.
column9: It looks to the near future: 我馬上來. 就 adds urgency: 馬上就到 "arriving any moment". It can look back too: 他馬上就走了 "he left right away". 馬 began as a picture of a horse facing left, its mane flowing in the wind.

column3: Clock hours: 三点, 三点半, and 几点 asks the time. Elsewhere 点菜 is "order dishes", 一点儿 "a bit", and 有点儿 "a little", mostly for something unwelcome: 有点儿贵.
column9: Clock hours: 三點, 三點半, and 幾點 asks the time. Elsewhere 點菜 is "order dishes", 一點兒 "a bit", and 有點兒 "a little", mostly for something unwelcome: 有點兒貴.

column3: It goes before the verb: 常来, 常去. 不常 means "not often", and 常常 and 经常 say the same a little more fully. 常 first meant a "lower garment", like a skirt, and was borrowed for "frequently".
column7: I often go to that shop.
column9: It goes before the verb: 常來, 常去. 不常 means "not often", and 常常 and 經常 say the same a little more fully. 常 first meant a "lower garment", like a skirt, and was borrowed for "frequently".

column3: Often, the doubled form of 常: 他常常来. The usual negative is 不常, not 不常常; 常常不 is something else, "often doesn't": 他常常不吃早饭. It goes before the verb.
column6: Tā chángcháng gěi wǒ dǎ diànhuà.
column9: Often, the doubled form of 常: 他常常來. The usual negative is 不常, not 不常常; 常常不 is something else, "often doesn't": 他常常不吃早飯. It goes before the verb.

column3: 先…再… and 先…然后… line up steps: 先吃饭，再看书. On its own, 你先走 means "you go ahead (and I will follow)". 先 puts a foot 止 with a person 儿, to go forward.
column9: 先…再… and 先…然後… line up steps: 先吃飯，再看書. On its own, 你先走 means "you go ahead (and I will follow)". 先 puts a foot 止 with a person 儿, to go forward.

column3: Again for something that has not happened yet: 再说一次 "say it once more". In 先…再… it means "then". For a repeat that already took place, Chinese uses 又 instead.
column9: Again for something that has not happened yet: 再說一次 "say it once more". In 先…再… it means "then". For a repeat that already took place, Chinese uses 又 instead.

column3: The last occasion, with no 个: 上次你去哪儿了？ The next one is 下次. For a week or month use 上周 and 上个月 instead. 次 began as a picture of a person exhaling.
column7: Where did you go last time?
column9: The last occasion, with no 個: 上次你去哪兒了？ The next one is 下次. For a week or month use 上周 and 上個月 instead. 次 began as a picture of a person exhaling.

column3: The next occasion, often a promise: 下次我请你. 下次再说 "let's talk about it another time" is also a polite way to put something off.
column9: The next occasion, often a promise: 下次我請你. 下次再說 "let's talk about it another time" is also a polite way to put something off.

column3: It also goes with medicine and more than food: 吃药, 吃苦 "bear hardship". Soup is drunk (喝汤), not eaten. 你吃了吗？ is a friendly greeting.
column9: It also goes with medicine and more than food: 吃藥, 吃苦 "bear hardship". Soup is drunk (喝湯), not eaten. 你吃了嗎？ is a friendly greeting.

column3: Anything drunk takes it, soup too: 喝水, 喝茶, 喝汤, and 喝酒 for alcohol. Soup is never 吃.
column7: What do you want to drink?
column9: Anything drunk takes it, soup too: 喝水, 喝茶, 喝湯, and 喝酒 for alcohol. Soup is never 吃.

column3: Cooked rice and any meal: 做饭 is "cook", 吃饭 "eat", and the three meals are 早饭, 午饭 and 晚饭. Rice by itself is 米饭. 饭 is the word for "what is eaten".
column9: Cooked rice and any meal: 做飯 is "cook", 吃飯 "eat", and the three meals are 早飯, 午飯 and 晚飯. Rice by itself is 米飯. 飯 is the word for "what is eaten".

column3: A dish to go with rice as well as greens: 点菜 orders dishes, 川菜 is Sichuan food, and 菜 is the usual word for food from a place. 菜 is literally "what is gathered or plucked".
column9: A dish to go with rice as well as greens: 點菜 orders dishes, 川菜 is Sichuan food, and 菜 is the usual word for food from a place. 菜 is literally "what is gathered or plucked".

column3: 喝茶 is the verb; 茶叶 is the leaves, 茶馆 a teahouse. 红茶 (red tea) is what English calls black tea, and 绿茶 is green tea. 茶 is a modified form of an older character for a "bitter plant".
column9: 喝茶 is the verb; 茶葉 is the leaves, 茶館 a teahouse. 紅茶 (red tea) is what English calls black tea, and 綠茶 is green tea. 茶 is a modified form of an older character for a "bitter plant".

column3: Plain water takes 喝水; 热水 is hot water and 开水 boiled water. 水 also starts 水果, and ends some old river names: 汉水, 淮水. 水 is a picture of flowing water, and next to another character it squeezes into 氵.
column9: Plain water takes 喝水; 熱水 is hot water and 開水 boiled water. 水 also starts 水果, and ends some old river names: 漢水, 淮水. 水 is a picture of flowing water, and next to another character it squeezes into 氵.

column3: Milk: 牛奶 is cow's milk. 女 (woman) is the meaning part and 乃 gives the sound, nǎi in both. 奶奶 "grandma" (the father's mother) uses it too.
column9: Milk: 牛奶 is cow's milk. 女 (woman) is the meaning part and 乃 gives the sound, nǎi in both. 奶奶 "grandma" (the father's mother) uses it too.

column3: The everyday word for milk: 喝牛奶. 奶 alone appears in 奶茶 (milk tea) and 奶酪 (cheese), and 牛奶 specifies that the milk is cow's. 牛 is a picture of a bull's head, with two horns and two ears.
column9: The everyday word for milk: 喝牛奶. 奶 alone appears in 奶茶 (milk tea) and 奶酪 (cheese), and 牛奶 specifies that the milk is cow's. 牛 is a picture of a bull's head, with two horns and two ears.

column3: The rice served with a meal, counted by the bowl: 一碗米饭. 米 alone is the raw grain, and 大米 is rice as a staple. 米 is a picture of rice kernels without the husk.
column9: The rice served with a meal, counted by the bowl: 一碗米飯. 米 alone is the raw grain, and 大米 is rice as a staple. 米 is a picture of rice kernels without the husk.

column3: Bread: 面 ("flour") plus 包 ("wrapped thing"). A slice is 一片面包, and to toast bread is 烤面包.
column7: I eat bread in the morning.
column9: Bread: 麵 ("flour") plus 包 ("wrapped thing"). A slice is 一片麵包, and to toast bread is 烤麵包.

column3: The 儿 is optional: 面条 is the same food. 面 alone also means noodles (牛肉面), and 条 is the measure word for long thin things. 面 is also the character for "face", a picture of a face with one eye exaggerated.
column9: The 兒 is optional: 麵條 is the same food. 麵 alone also means noodles (牛肉麵), and 條 is the measure word for long thin things. 麵 is also the character for "face", a picture of a face with one eye exaggerated.

column3: It has a filling, unlike plain 馒头: 肉包子, 菜包子. The 子 is light: bāozi. 包 pictures a baby 巳 in the womb 勹, or a swaddled baby.
column6: Wǒ xiǎng chī liǎng ge bāozi.
column7: I'd like to eat two buns.
column9: It has a filling, unlike plain 饅頭: 肉包子, 菜包子. The 子 is light: bāozi. 包 pictures a baby 巳 in the womb 勹, or a swaddled baby.

column3: Name the animal first: 牛肉, 猪肉, 羊肉. Alone it is meat in general, and 肉 is also the flesh of a fruit: 果肉. 肉 pictures the ribs of an animal or a slice of meat, and takes the shape 月 next to a sound part.
column9: Name the animal first: 牛肉, 豬肉, 羊肉. Alone it is meat in general, and 肉 is also the flesh of a fruit: 果肉. 肉 pictures the ribs of an animal or a slice of meat, and takes the shape 月 next to a sound part.

column3: Cooking words come before it: 煮鸡蛋 "boiled egg", 炒鸡蛋 "scrambled egg"; count them with 个. 蛋 alone is any egg, so a duck egg is 鸭蛋. 蛋 was coined late, and its 虫 stands for snake or insect, with snake eggs in particular.
column6: Wǒ zǎofàn chī yī ge jīdàn.
column7: I eat an egg at breakfast.
column9: Cooking words come before it: 煮雞蛋 "boiled egg", 炒雞蛋 "scrambled egg"; count them with 個. 蛋 alone is any egg, so a duck egg is 鴨蛋. 蛋 was coined late, and its 虫 stands for snake or insect, with snake eggs in particular.

column3: Fruit as a food or a kind of shop: 吃水果, 水果店. To name one fruit, use its own word: 苹果, 香蕉. 果 is a picture of fruit on a tree.
column9: Fruit as a food or a kind of shop: 吃水果, 水果店. To name one fruit, use its own word: 蘋果, 香蕉. 果 is a picture of fruit on a tree.

column3: 好 plus a verb gives "good to…": 好看, 好听, 好玩儿, and 好喝 for drinks. The opposite is 难吃. 好 puts a woman 女 with a child 子: it was good for a woman to have a child.
column9: 好 plus a verb gives "good to…": 好看, 好聽, 好玩兒, and 好喝 for drinks. The opposite is 難吃. 好 puts a woman 女 with a child 子: it was good for a woman to have a child.

column3: A verb and its object, so it splits: 吃了饭 "have eaten", 吃过饭 "have eaten before". 你吃饭了吗？ asks if someone has eaten.
column9: A verb and its object, so it splits: 吃了飯 "have eaten", 吃過飯 "have eaten before". 你吃飯了嗎？ asks if someone has eaten.

column3: The first of three meals: 早饭, 午饭, 晚饭. 早饭 is everyday mainland speech; in Taiwan 早餐 is the everyday word, and on the mainland it is more formal. 早 began as a picture of an acorn and was borrowed for the sound of "morning".
column9: The first of three meals: 早飯, 午飯, 晚飯. 早飯 is everyday mainland speech; in Taiwan 早餐 is the everyday word, and on the mainland it is more formal. 早 began as a picture of an acorn and was borrowed for the sound of "morning".

column3: Lunch: 吃午饭. 午饭 and 中饭 are everyday mainland speech; in Taiwan 午餐 or 中餐 is the everyday word, and on the mainland 午餐 is more formal. 午 began as a picture of a pestle and has nothing to do with 干.
column9: Lunch: 吃午飯. 午飯 and 中飯 are everyday mainland speech; in Taiwan 午餐 or 中餐 is the everyday word, and on the mainland 午餐 is more formal. 午 began as a picture of a pestle and has nothing to do with 干.

column3: Dinner, supper: 晚 ("evening") plus 饭. The verb is 吃: 吃晚饭.
column9: Dinner, supper: 晚 ("evening") plus 飯. The verb is 吃: 吃晚飯.

column3: 杯 alone is the measure word: 一杯水, 一杯茶. The 子 makes it a noun and is light: bēizi. A teacup is 茶杯.
column7: There is water in the cup.
column9: 杯 alone is the measure word: 一杯水, 一杯茶. The 子 makes it a noun and is light: bēizi. A teacup is 茶杯.

column3: It links an owner or a description to a noun: 我的书, 新的书. It sounds like 得 and 地, but 地 goes before a verb (慢慢地走) and 得 after one (走得快). 的 began as 旳, meaning "bright".
column9: It links an owner or a description to a noun: 我的書, 新的書. It sounds like 得 and 地, but 地 goes before a verb (慢慢地走) and 得 after one (走得快). 的 began as 旳, meaning "bright".

column3: A light particle: after a verb 我吃了饭, at the end 下雨了 "it has started to rain". It marks completion or change, not simply the past. 了 is said to be a picture of a baby without arms.
column6: Wǒ chī le liǎng ge bāozi.
column9: A light particle: after a verb 我吃了飯, at the end 下雨了 "it has started to rain". It marks completion or change, not simply the past. 了 is said to be a picture of a baby without arms.

column3: It turns a statement into a yes/no question: 你有哥哥吗？ Never add a question word such as 什么 or 谁 to it. The particle is said to come from an old word for "not".
column7: Do you have an older brother?
column9: It turns a statement into a yes/no question: 你有哥哥嗎？ Never add a question word such as 什麼 or 誰 to it. The particle is said to come from an old word for "not".

column3: And what about…?: 我很好，你呢？ It asks where something is: 我的书呢？ After 在 or 正在 it adds "right now": 他在吃饭呢.
column9: And what about…?: 我很好，你呢？ It asks where something is: 我的書呢？ After 在 or 正在 it adds "right now": 他在吃飯呢.

column3: It softens a suggestion: 我们走吧 "let's go". It also asks for confirmation: 他是老师吧？ "he is a teacher, right?"
column9: It softens a suggestion: 我們走吧 "let's go". It also asks for confirmation: 他是老師吧？ "he is a teacher, right?"

column3: A light particle after a verb that says a state continues: 门开着 "the door is open", 他坐着 "he is sitting". Taiwan writes it 著; 着, the mainland's form, is not used there.
column9: A light particle after a verb that says a state continues: 門開著 "the door is open", 他坐著 "he is sitting". Taiwan writes it 著; 著, the mainland's form, is not used there.

column3: 1. A particle after a verb, saying you have done it before: 我去过北京 "I have been to Beijing"; the negative is 没去过. 2. A verb, "pass, spend": 过年, 经过, 度过. 辶 (walk) is the meaning part.
column9: 1. A particle after a verb, saying you have done it before: 我去過北京 "I have been to Beijing"; the negative is 沒去過. 2. A verb, "pass, spend": 過年, 經過, 度過. 辶 (walk) is the meaning part.

column3: It turns a describing word into an adverb right before the verb: 慢慢地走 "walk slowly". It sounds like 的 and 得, so check where it sits. An early form of 地 showed a hill, a pig and a mound of earth.
column9: It turns a describing word into an adverb right before the verb: 慢慢地走 "walk slowly". It sounds like 的 and 得, so check where it sits. An early form of 地 showed a hill, a pig and a mound of earth.

column3: Right away, as early as, just: 我马上就来; 他八点就来了 "he came already at eight", earlier than expected. 才 is the opposite: 他八点才来 "he didn't come until eight". 就 usually comes with 了, and 才 does not. It goes before the verb.
column6: Tā bā diǎn jiù qǐchuáng le.
column7: He was already up at eight.
column9: Right away, as early as, just: 我馬上就來; 他八點就來了 "he came already at eight", earlier than expected. 才 is the opposite: 他八點才來 "he didn't come until eight". 就 usually comes with 了, and 才 does not. It goes before the verb.

column3: Before a verb: 他还在家 "he is still at home", and 还有 "and there is also". Before an adjective, 还不错 means "pretty good".
column9: Before a verb: 他還在家 "he is still at home", and 還有 "and there is also". Before an adjective, 還不錯 means "pretty good".

column3: Before a verb it says the action is going on: 他正看书呢, with 呢 at the end for a spoken feel. It also means "exactly": 正好 "just right".
column9: Before a verb it says the action is going on: 他正看書呢, with 呢 at the end for a spoken feel. It also means "exactly": 正好 "just right".

column3: It stresses "right now": 我正在吃饭. 在 alone can mark this too. The negative uses 没: 他没在睡觉 "he is not sleeping".
column9: It stresses "right now": 我正在吃飯. 在 alone can mark this too. The negative uses 沒: 他沒在睡覺 "he is not sleeping".

column3: Before a verb it is a command: 别说话. It is the spoken word for 不要. 别人 and 别的 mean "other people" and "other"; 别客气 says "don't stand on ceremony". 别 began as 冎 (bone) and 刀-knife 刂, to cut up bone and flesh.
column9: Before a verb it is a command: 別說話. It is the spoken word for 不要. 別人 and 別的 mean "other people" and "other"; 別客氣 says "don't stand on ceremony". 別 began as 冎 (bone) and 刀-knife 刂, to cut up bone and flesh.

column3: Some (of them): 有的人 "some people". Often paired: 有的…，有的… "some…, others…". The 的 is light: yǒude.
column9: Some (of them): 有的人 "some people". Often paired: 有的…，有的… "some…, others…". The 的 is light: yǒude.

column3: It points toward the speaker: 他来了. After a verb it gives direction: 回来, 拿来. Before a verb it means "I will do it": 我来介绍一下. 来 began as a picture of wheat, with the ear in the middle and roots below.
column9: It points toward the speaker: 他來了. After a verb it gives direction: 回來, 拿來. Before a verb it means "I will do it": 我來介紹一下. 來 began as a picture of wheat, with the ear in the middle and roots below.

column3: A place follows directly, with no 到: 去学校, 去北京. 去 plus a verb is "go and do it": 去吃饭. After a verb it points away from the speaker: 回去.
column9: A place follows directly, with no 到: 去學校, 去北京. 去 plus a verb is "go and do it": 去吃飯. After a verb it points away from the speaker: 回去.

column3: 回家, 回学校. With a direction it gives 回来 and 回去. 回 also counts occasions: 去过两回 "been twice". 回 began as a picture of rotation, once a spiral.
column7: What time do you go home?
column9: 回家, 回學校. With a direction it gives 回來 and 回去. 回 also counts occasions: 去過兩回 "been twice". 回 began as a picture of rotation, once a spiral.

column3: 到 plus a place is "arrive": 到北京, 到家. After a verb it shows the goal was met: 看到, 找到. With a time it means "until": 到七点.
column9: 到 plus a place is "arrive": 到北京, 到家. After a verb it shows the goal was met: 看到, 找到. With a time it means "until": 到七點.

column3: Enter: 进门; 进来 "come in", 进去 "go in". 辶 (walk) is the meaning part. The opposite is 出: 出门, 出去 "go out".
column9: Enter: 進門; 進來 "come in", 進去 "go in". 辶 (walk) is the meaning part. The opposite is 出: 出門, 出去 "go out".

column3: 出门 is "leave home". After a verb it shows direction: 拿出来, 走出去. 出来 is toward the speaker, 出去 away from them. 出 was a foot 止 stepping out of a cave 凵, though the character later lost its original shape.
column9: 出門 is "leave home". After a verb it shows direction: 拿出來, 走出去. 出來 is toward the speaker, 出去 away from them. 出 was a foot 止 stepping out of a cave 凵, though the character later lost its original shape.

column3: In Chinese it is "walk", not "run" (that is 跑): 走路. 我走了 "I'm off". With a place it is "go by foot": 走到学校. 走 began as a picture of a running man, with a foot 止 added later.
column9: In Chinese it is "walk", not "run" (that is 跑): 走路. 我走了 "I'm off". With a place it is "go by foot": 走到學校. 走 began as a picture of a running man, with a foot 止 added later.

column3: 跑步 is running or jogging as exercise, and 跑腿 is running an errand. After a verb 跑 means away, as in 逃跑 and 吓跑, where it is about getting off, not speed. Its computing sense, as in running a program, is a semantic loan from English run.
column7: The child is running on the road.
column9: 跑步 is running or jogging as exercise, and 跑腿 is running an errand. After a verb 跑 means away, as in 逃跑 and 嚇跑, where it is about getting off, not speed. Its computing sense, as in running a program, is a semantic loan from English run.

column3: Used for travel in a vehicle you sit in: 坐车, 坐飞机, 坐地铁. For a bike or a horse you straddle, say 骑. 请坐 invites a guest to take a seat, and 坐着 means be seated.
column7: I go to Beijing by train.
column9: Used for travel in a vehicle you sit in: 坐車, 坐飛機, 坐地鐵. For a bike or a horse you straddle, say 騎. 請坐 invites a guest to take a seat, and 坐著 means be seated.

column3: Also a stop or station: 车站, and 站台 is the platform. 站住 means stop right there, and 站着 is standing, as against 坐着.
column7: He is standing at the door.
column9: Also a stop or station: 車站, and 站臺 is the platform. 站住 means stop right there, and 站著 is standing, as against 坐著.

column3: Arrive at, come to: 来到北京 "come to Beijing". A place follows directly. It is 来 plus 到, "come and arrive".
column9: Arrive at, come to: 來到北京 "come to Beijing". A place follows directly. It is 來 plus 到, "come and arrive".

column3: Coming back to where the speaker is or will be: 他回来了 means he is back. After a verb it adds the same direction: 带回来 'bring back'. 来 began as a picture of wheat, and has been borrowed for 'to come' since the oracle bone script.
column9: Coming back to where the speaker is or will be: 他回來了 means he is back. After a verb it adds the same direction: 帶回來 'bring back'. 來 began as a picture of wheat, and has been borrowed for 'to come' since the oracle bone script.

column3: Going back away from the speaker, to where you came from: 我要回去了 'I have to head back'. 带回去 'take back' pairs with 带回来 'bring back'. 去 comes from a Sino-Tibetan word whose basic meaning was 'to get rid of'.
column6: Tài wǎn le, wǒ yào huíqu le.
column7: It's late, I have to go back.
column9: Going back away from the speaker, to where you came from: 我要回去了 'I have to head back'. 帶回去 'take back' pairs with 帶回來 'bring back'. 去 comes from a Sino-Tibetan word whose basic meaning was 'to get rid of'.

column3: 回 takes 家 directly, with no 去 needed: 我回家. 回到家 works too, and 回家去 and 回家来 add a direction. Being there, rather than going, is 在家.
column9: 回 takes 家 directly, with no 去 needed: 我回家. 回到家 works too, and 回家去 and 回家來 add a direction. Being there, rather than going, is 在家.

column3: Return to: 回到家 "get back home". 到 says the place was reached; a place follows.
column9: Return to: 回到家 "get back home". 到 says the place was reached; a place follows.

column3: Come in toward the speaker, who is already inside: 请进来. After other verbs it adds the inward direction: 走进来, 跑进来, 搬进来 'move in'.
column7: Please come in and sit down.
column9: Come in toward the speaker, who is already inside: 請進來. After other verbs it adds the inward direction: 走進來, 跑進來, 搬進來 'move in'.

column3: Go in, away from the speaker, who is outside: 你先进去吧. After a verb it adds the inward direction: 走进去, 放进去 'put in'.
column9: Go in, away from the speaker, who is outside: 你先進去吧. After a verb it adds the inward direction: 走進去, 放進去 'put in'.

column3: Come out toward the speaker. After a verb it can mean noticing or producing: 看出来 'make out', 想出来 'think of'. 出 began as a foot 止 stepping out of a cave 凵; the sprout reading is a later misreading.
column7: He came out of the house.
column9: Come out toward the speaker. After a verb it can mean noticing or producing: 看出來 'make out', 想出來 'think of'. 出 began as a foot 止 stepping out of a cave 凵; the sprout reading is a later misreading.

column3: Go out, away from the speaker: 出去玩 'go out for fun', 我出去一下 'I'll step out'. After a verb it adds the outward direction: 跑出去, 拿出去 'take out'. The 土 on top of 去 is a man shape simplified, as in 赤 and 走.
column7: I'm going out to buy things.
